title: Religious Young Men Are Happier, Healthier, and More Successful
gist: Using the April 2025 IFS Young Men’s Survey, Ken Burchfiel finds that men aged 18-29 who attend religious services weekly are markedly more likely than secular peers to be married (27% vs 9%), very happy (41% vs 24%), degree-holders (46% vs 16%) and to have three or more close friends — yet only 18% of young men attend weekly and 53% rarely or never do. He cautions the data are cross-sectional and evidence of a Gen Z male religious revival remains limited.

insights.claim: Around 4 in 10 American men aged 18-29 have fewer than three close friends, around half believe people like them will never achieve the American dream no matter how hard they work, and 42% feel like a failure.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Widespread demoralization among young men is a risk to labor-force engagement, family formation and social stability.

insights.claim: Marriage rates for 18- to 29-year-old men have dropped considerably over the last 60 years, and a majority of these men feel isolated or lonely at least some of the time.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Declining young-male marriage feeds delayed household formation and lower fertility.

themes.theme: Religion and marriage among young men

insights.claim: 27% of religious (weekly-attending) men aged 18-29 are married versus just 9% of secular men, and 94% of weekly attenders are married or want to be versus 63% of those attending less than yearly.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Religious young men are a much stronger pipeline for marriage and household formation.

insights.claim: About half of religious young men are not in a romantic relationship, versus around two-thirds of secular young men; religious young men are also more likely to have or want children.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Even among the religious, partnering is difficult; secular men face a deeper partnering deficit with implications for fertility.

insights.claim: Across Protestants, Catholics and other faiths, young men who attend services weekly are more likely to be married or want marriage than co-believers who attend less often, so attendance rather than belief alone tracks outcomes.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Practice and community participation, not mere affiliation, appear to be the operative variable.

insights.claim: Contrary to assumptions that religious rules hamper flourishing, 41% of religious young men are 'very happy' versus 24% of secular men, and secular men are more than twice as likely to report fair or poor mental health (35% vs 15%).
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Religious participation is associated with materially better mental health among young men.
insights.quote: Secular men are also more than twice as likely to report fair or poor mental health (35%) as religious men (15%).
insights.locator: Religious Young Men Have Better Well-Being

insights.claim: About two-thirds of religious young men say their life has purpose or meaning versus only 4 in 10 secular men, and active depression and anxiety are more common among secular men.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Meaning deficit among secular young men may underlie broader mental-health demand.

insights.claim: General Social Survey data show that in most decades since the 1970s, including the 2020s, men aged 18-29 attending services weekly are significantly happier than those attending less than yearly, even controlling for age, race, education and marital status.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: The religion-happiness link is a persistent, multi-decade pattern rather than a recent artifact.
insights.locator: The link between religious service attendance and happiness

insights.claim: Among men aged 25-64, married weekly attenders have been happier than unmarried weekly attenders every decade since the 1970s, and religious married men are happier than nominal and secular married men in every decade except the 2010s.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Marriage and religious attendance appear to add independently to male happiness.

insights.claim: Despite Barna Research finding about 7 in 10 Christian students finish college with diminished or no faith, religious young men are far more likely to hold a bachelor's degree (46%) than nominal (29%) or secular men (16%).
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Challenges the assumption that education and religiosity are inversely related among young men.
insights.quote: Religious young men are far more likely (46%) to have a bachelor’s degree than nominal (29%) and secular men (16%).
insights.locator: Religious Young Men Have Better Education Outcomes

insights.claim: 29% of religious young men have finished trade school or an apprenticeship versus 14% of secular young men; among men aged 24-29 the figures are 36% vs 16%.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Religious young men show stronger human-capital accumulation across both academic and vocational tracks.

insights.claim: The education gap is not an age artifact: weekly attendance does not differ significantly between men aged 18-23 and 24-29, and among 24-29 year-olds 61% of religious men hold a bachelor's degree versus 40% of nominal and 25% of secular men.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Strengthens the robustness of the religion-education association.

insights.claim: College-educated young men attend religious services weekly at 33%, versus 20% of men pursuing a bachelor's and 13% of all other men, calling into question the assumption that highly educated people are less religious.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Religiosity among young men may be concentrating in the educated, higher-earning segment.
insights.quote: These findings call into question the assumption, at least for young men, “that highly educated people are less religious.”

insights.claim: 68% of young men attending services weekly have three or more close friends versus 52% of those who rarely or never attend, and religious young men are less likely to be lonely (18% vs 29%).
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Congregations function as friendship infrastructure in an era of male loneliness.
insights.locator: Weekly Service Attendance is Linked to More Friends

insights.claim: Citing Chaeyoon Lim and Robert Putnam, the author argues congregation-based friendships raise life satisfaction beyond friend count alone, but only when a strong religious identity is present — so the nature, not just quantity, of religious friendships matters.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Suggests the well-being benefit is not easily replicated by secular social networks.

themes.theme: Weekly attendance is a shrinking minority

insights.claim: Only 18% of men aged 18-29 attend religious services weekly, while 53% attend less than once a year or not at all; current-decade weekly attendance is lower than in the 1970s-1990s.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: The protective factor identified covers a small and declining share of young men.
insights.locator: Religious Young Men Are a Minority

insights.claim: Weekly attendance among young men is 28% for conservatives versus 14% for moderates and 17% for liberals, higher for employed men, 32% for married versus 16% for unmarried, and 22% for those whose parents were married at age 16 versus 13% otherwise.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Religiosity clusters with conservatism, employment and intact family background, reinforcing class and political sorting.
insights.locator: Certain groups of young men are more likely

insights.claim: The survey is cross-sectional, so causality is unproven: marriage could drive attendance rather than the reverse, or a third variable such as political preference could shape both.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: Investors and policymakers should treat the religion-outcome gaps as correlations, not levers.
insights.quote: it’s possible that marriage makes individuals more likely to attend religious services weekly, and not the other way around
insights.locator: Conclusion

insights.claim: Anecdotes suggest a possible return to faith among younger men, but evidence for a revival is limited; if Gen Z men do return to the pews, their well-being, social lives and marriage prospects may improve.
insights.speaker: Ken Burchfiel
insights.so_what: A reported Gen Z male religious revival is not yet visible in attendance data — treat claims skeptically.
insights.quote: The evidence for such a revival is limited
